summary: This informational RFC describes a test for whether an application can establish sessions quickly and reliably in complex environments, like dual-stack or IPv6 networks with multiple prefixes. Slow session setup is a barrier to IPv6 deployment.

plainLanguage.summary: A test to check whether a program connects fast even when the internet is a bit messy, and does not leave users staring at a spinner.

questions: how to test dual stack connection speed
subtitle: How to measure whether apps connect quickly in dual-stack networks.

tldr.problem: When computers have both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, applications may try each address in sequence, causing users to wait several seconds or more for a connection to establish. This slow setup discourages IPv6 deployment.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6556 defines a test that measures how long it takes an application to establish a session with a server when multiple addresses are available, simulating various network failures to see how the application responds.
tldr.outcome: The test reveals whether an application tries addresses in parallel or serially, and how quickly it succeeds under best-case and worst-case conditions.

today: RFC 6556 is an Internet Standard informational document published in April 2012 and remains the reference for testing session setup time in dual-stack networks. It defines a laboratory test methodology that is widely used by vendors and ISPs to evaluate whether applications and systems implement quick session establishment efficiently.

sections.title: The Dual-Stack Problem
sections.content:
When a computer is dual-stack (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6), and networks have filtering rules like BCP 38 ingress filtering, not all address combinations will work. A naive application using the sockets API might retrieve a list of addresses for a peer using getaddrinfo() and try them one by one until one succeeds. If the application waits for a TCP timeout before trying the next address, users may wait several seconds—or longer—to connect.

RFC 6555 (Happy Eyeballs) addresses this by proposing algorithms that try multiple addresses in parallel or with short delays. RFC 6556 provides a way to measure whether applications and systems implement this behavior well.
sections.plainLanguage: When you connect to a website, you might get four addresses to try. If the program tries them one at a time and waits for timeouts, it is slow. If it tries them at the same time or with short delays, it is fast. This RFC measures which one an app does.

sections.title: What the Test Measures
sections.content:
The test is a black box measurement: it does not test a specific algorithm, but the observable behavior of the application and its host system. The goal is to measure how long it takes from the moment an application makes its first DNS request until a session is successfully established.

The test works with any transport protocol (TCP, UDP, or others). For TCP, the session is established when the three-way handshake completes. For UDP, it is when the first response is received. The measurement assumes that initial session setup is limited by DNS queries and transport-layer handshaking.
sections.plainLanguage: The test is like a stopwatch: it measures the total time from 'I ask for the address' to 'I have a working connection.' It does not care what trick the program uses, just how long it takes.

sections.title: The Test Laboratory Setup
sections.content:
The test requires a controlled laboratory with four main components: Alice (the client application being tested), Bob (the server), a DNS server, and a protocol analyzer (such as tcpdump).

Alice and Bob each have both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Router 1 sits between Alice and Bob and is configured to block one route at a time using techniques such as silently dropping packets, responding with ICMP errors, installing null routes, or sending TCP RST messages. The tester runs the measurement once for each of Bob's addresses, blocking all but one route per test run.

The configuration tests various failure modes, including Path MTU Discovery issues, to see how the application responds to different kinds of network problems.
sections.plainLanguage: You set up a fake network in the lab where the server has multiple addresses, and you block them one by one to see how the client program handles it. You also trick it with fake errors to see if it gives up too fast or waits too long.

sections.title: How to Run the Test
sections.content:
On each test run, Alice initiates a session to Bob. The protocol analyzer records all traffic at Alice's network interface. The tester observes the sequence of DNS requests and connection attempts (TCP SYNs or equivalent), noting whether multiple addresses are tried in parallel or serially.

If the DNS server randomizes address order or if addresses come back in different orders on successive queries, the test may need to run multiple times until each of Bob's addresses has appeared as the first (or early) choice in the DNS response, ensuring that each address is actually tried.

The tester may flush the resolver cache between iterations to force DNS re-resolution, or wait for the DNS TTL to expire naturally.
sections.plainLanguage: You run the test many times, blocking different addresses each time. You record everything the program does, watching for pattern: does it try all addresses at once, or does it wait between attempts?

sections.title: Metrics and Results
sections.content:
Three main metrics are measured, all in milliseconds:

Session Setup Interval: The time from the first DNS query to successful connection establishment. Measured for each test run.

Minimum Session Setup Interval: The fastest connection time observed, usually the case where the first address tried succeeds immediately.

Maximum Session Setup Interval: The slowest connection time observed, usually when the first (or early) addresses fail and the application must try all addresses before one succeeds. If the application gives up before connecting, the interval is infinite.

A fourth metric, the Attempt Pattern, is descriptive: a narrative of how the application attempts connections. For example: 'TCP SYNs to new addresses every 250 milliseconds' or 'IPv6 SYNs every 200 ms, IPv4 SYNs every 300 ms, independent sequences.'

Timing precision must be better than 0.1 milliseconds over 60 seconds (1 part per million).
sections.plainLanguage: The results answer three questions: How long was the fastest connection? How long was the slowest? What pattern did the program follow when trying addresses?
